body:
Why maps use symbols

A map cannot show every road, building, tree, railway or water body in its actual shape and size. Instead, simplified signs, letters, lines, patterns and colours are used to represent geographical features.

Widely recognised or standardised signs are called conventional symbols. They allow a map to communicate considerable information within a limited space.

The legend, also called the key, explains the symbols used on a particular map. Symbols may differ between mapping organisations, countries, map editions and map purposes. The legend therefore takes priority over assumptions about a symbol.

Point, line and area symbols

Symbol typeInformation representedExamples
PointLocation of a featureWell, post office, spot height
LineLinear extent or connectionRiver, road, railway, boundary
AreaExtent of a geographical featureForest, lake, cultivated land

The method used to represent a feature also depends on scale. A city may appear as a point on an atlas map but as an extensive built-up area on a large-scale topographical map.

Conventional colours on Indian topographical maps

The Survey of India prepares and publishes topographical maps of India and provides conventional signs for their interpretation. The following colour associations are commonly used on traditional Indian topographical sheets.

ColourTypical representation
BlueWater features
BrownContours and relief features
GreenVegetation and forest features
BlackRailways and many other cultural symbols
RedCertain roads and settlements
YellowCultivated land on many traditional sheets

In ordinary school physical maps, green commonly represents low-lying plains, yellow may represent intermediate elevations or plateaus, and brown represents higher relief. These colours describe elevation rather than necessarily describing vegetation or land use.

Map colours do not have a single universal meaning. Green may represent low elevation on a physical map but vegetation on a topographical map. Always interpret colours according to the map's legend and purpose.

Important symbols and abbreviations

Traditional Indian topographical maps use several standard abbreviations for buildings, facilities, forests and elevation measurements.

AbbreviationMeaning
POPost Office
PTOPost and Telegraph Office
PSPolice Station
RSRailway Station
RHRest House
CHCircuit House
BMBench Mark
RFReserved Forest
PFProtected Forest

A spot height is commonly shown by a dot accompanied by an elevation value, such as a dot marked 152 m. A triangulation station is commonly represented by a triangle accompanied by an elevation value. A bench mark may be identified by BM and its recorded elevation.

The abbreviation RF has 2 distinct meanings in map studies. In scale calculations, it means representative fraction. When used as a forest annotation on a traditional topographical sheet, it can mean reserved forest.

Recognising features through their symbols

Traditional map conventions distinguish lined wells from unlined wells, perennial streams from non-perennial streams, metalled roads from unmetalled roads, and different categories of administrative boundaries.

For example, an unlined well may be represented by a small open circle, while a lined well may be represented by a filled circle in conventional school topographical legends.

A perennial stream contains flowing water throughout the year under normal conditions, while a non-perennial stream does not. Traditional maps commonly distinguish them through different line patterns, such as continuous and broken lines.

Interpreting a legend in a map question

When a map includes unfamiliar lines, shaded areas or symbols, examine the legend before identifying geographical features. A broken line could represent a seasonal stream, a footpath or a particular boundary depending on its colour, pattern and the key provided.

The absence of a particular symbol does not always prove that the corresponding feature is absent from the ground. It may have been omitted because of the map's scale, date or purpose.

Prelims focus

  • Conventional symbols are standardised representations of geographical features.
  • A legend explains the meaning of map symbols and colours.
  • Brown commonly represents contours on topographical sheets.
  • Blue commonly represents water features.
  • PO means Post Office, whereas PS means Police Station.
  • Trap: RF can mean representative fraction or reserved forest, depending on the context.

[References: NCERT, The Earth: Our Habitat, Class 6, 2018-19, Chapter 4, Maps, p. 26 and Figure 4.3; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Grade 6, Chapter 1, pp. 11-12 and Figure 1.2; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 15, pp. 114-115, and Chapter 17, pp. 125-129, consulted 26 November 2026; Survey of India, Conventional Signs for Topographical Maps on Metric System, 2nd edition, 1990, Water Features and Heights, Trigonometrical Symbols and Abbreviations, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Conventional Symbols, Colours and Map Legends

body:
Meaning of relief

The Earth's surface contains mountains, hills, plateaus, valleys, plains and depressions. The differences in elevation and shape of the land surface are collectively described as relief.

Relief representation allows a flat map to communicate the three-dimensional character of the landscape.

Methods of representing relief

Layer tinting

Layer tinting uses different colours or shades to represent different elevation ranges. The legend indicates the elevation represented by each colour. It is useful for understanding the general distribution of lowlands, uplands and mountains.

Hill shading

Hill shading creates an impression of relief by representing the effects of light and shadow on slopes. It makes landforms easier to recognise visually but does not independently provide precise elevation values.

Hachures

Hachures are short lines drawn in the direction of slope. Their arrangement helps represent the general steepness and shape of the terrain.

Spot heights and bench marks

A spot height provides the elevation of an individual point. A bench mark identifies a fixed reference point whose elevation has been accurately established.

These methods provide information about specific locations but do not continuously represent the shape of the surrounding land.

Contours

Contours provide information about both elevation and the shape of the land surface. They are an important method of relief representation on topographical maps.

A contour line is an imaginary line joining points of equal elevation above a common reference level, normally mean sea level on ordinary land topographical maps.

Contour interval and horizontal equivalent

The contour interval, also called the vertical interval, is the difference in elevation between consecutive contour lines.

For example, if successive contours are marked 100 m, 120 m, 140 m and 160 m, the contour interval is 20 m.

The contour interval is normally constant throughout a particular contour map, unless otherwise indicated. Different maps may use different contour intervals depending on scale, terrain and mapping requirements.

The horizontal equivalent is the horizontal ground distance between adjacent contours. Unlike the vertical interval, it can vary from one part of the map to another.

Where contours are closer together, the same vertical change occurs over a shorter horizontal distance. The ground is therefore steeper. Where contours are farther apart, the same vertical change occurs over a longer horizontal distance, indicating a gentler slope.

Important properties of contours

  • All points on a single contour have the same elevation.
  • Contours represent imaginary lines, not physical lines on the ground.
  • Contours normally form closed loops, although part of a loop may extend beyond the map boundary.
  • Contours of different elevations normally do not intersect.
  • Contours may appear to merge where a nearly vertical cliff is represented.
  • Contour spacing indicates the steepness of the slope when the scale and contour interval are known.

Index contours

Selected contours are often drawn more prominently and labelled with their elevation values. These are called index contours. Intermediate contours between them help represent smaller differences in elevation.

Index contours make it easier to determine the elevation of unlabelled contours using the contour interval.

Determining elevation from contours

If 4 successive contour lines are marked 100 m, 120 m, 140 m and 160 m, the total elevation difference between the first and last lines is 60 m. There are 3 intervals between the 4 lines.

A point located between the 120 m and 140 m contours on an ordinary continuously rising slope has an elevation between 120 m and 140 m. Its exact elevation cannot be determined solely from the 2 contour lines.

Count the spaces between successive contours when calculating total elevation difference. Do not multiply the contour interval by the total number of contour lines.

Prelims focus

  • Contours join points of equal elevation.
  • Contour interval measures vertical elevation difference.
  • Horizontal equivalent measures horizontal distance between adjacent contours.
  • Contour interval is normally constant on a given map.
  • Index contours are emphasised contours with elevation information.
  • Trap: Closely spaced contours do not indicate a greater contour interval; they indicate a steeper slope when the interval is unchanged.

[References: NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 5, Topographical Maps, pp. 50-53; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 17, Topographical Sheets, pp. 124-125, consulted 26 November 2026; U.S. Geological Survey, US Topo Cartographic Specifications: Map Symbol Guide, Contours, consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Relief Representation and Fundamentals of Contours

body:
Understanding contour patterns

Contour lines represent the shape and elevation of terrain. By examining their spacing, arrangement and numerical values, a reader can identify hills, depressions, plateaus and different types of slopes.

A contour interval of 20 m means that each consecutive contour represents a vertical elevation difference of 20 m. The spacing between those contours reveals how rapidly the elevation changes horizontally.

Types of slopes

Gentle and steep slopes

A gentle slope has a relatively small change in elevation over a given horizontal distance. Its contours are widely spaced.

A steep slope has a relatively large change in elevation over a given horizontal distance. Its contours are closely spaced.

Uniform slope

A uniform slope maintains approximately the same steepness along its length. It is represented by contours that are approximately equally spaced, provided the contour interval is constant.

Concave slope

A concave slope is steeper in its upper part and gentler towards its lower part. Its contours are closely spaced at higher elevations and widely spaced at lower elevations.

Convex slope

A convex slope is gentler in its upper part and steeper towards its lower part. Its contours are widely spaced at higher elevations and closely spaced at lower elevations.

Identify the higher and lower elevations before distinguishing concave and convex slopes. The position of contours on the page alone does not indicate which part of the slope is higher.

Identifying hills and peaks

A hill is represented by closed contour loops whose elevations increase towards the centre.

A hill with approximately regular contour spacing and a narrow summit may represent a conical hill.

Consider a hill with closed contours of 100 m, 120 m and 140 m, increasing towards the centre. Its contour interval is 20 m. If the contour map is complete and no 160 m contour exists inside the 140 m contour, the summit lies at or above 140 m but below 160 m.

If a spot height of 152 m is marked at the summit, the elevation of that point is known more precisely.

Identifying depressions

A depression is an area of land that lies below its surrounding terrain. It may also be represented by closed contour loops, but their elevation values decrease towards the centre.

On maps that use depression contours, short inward-pointing marks may be attached to the closed contour lines to distinguish depressions from hills.

Closed contours alone are therefore insufficient to distinguish a hill from a depression. Their elevation values and any relevant depression markings must be examined.

Identifying plateaus and cliffs

A plateau is an elevated area with a relatively broad, level or gently undulating upper surface. Contours may be closely spaced around its steep margins, while the interior shows relatively little change in elevation.

A cliff is a very steep or nearly vertical land surface. Its contours appear extremely close together and may merge on the map.

Contour profiles

A contour map presents terrain from above. A topographic profile, also called a cross-section, presents a side view of the terrain along a selected line.

The profile reveals the changes in elevation that occur along that line. A rapidly rising profile represents a steep slope, while a gradually rising profile represents a gentle slope.

A contour map and its corresponding profile represent the same terrain from different viewpoints.

Prelims focus

  • Uniformly spaced contours indicate an approximately uniform slope.
  • Concave slopes are steeper above and gentler below.
  • Convex slopes are gentler above and steeper below.
  • Closed contours with elevations increasing inward indicate a hill.
  • A plateau generally has a broad upper surface and comparatively steep margins.
  • Trap: Every closed contour pattern does not necessarily represent a hill.

[References: NCERT, Practical Work in Geography, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 5, Topographical Maps, pp. 53-60; Arizona State University, Topographic and Geologic Maps, Figure 4-3, Examples of Topographic Features on Contour Maps, p. 3, consulted 26 November 2026.]
